Brecon
BREK-un
n. (the mid-Welsh county town and its county, holding Trevecca, the family seat of Howell Harris and the cradle of the Welsh revival of 1735)
Welsh Aberhonddu, the mouth of the Honddu; the English Brecon is from Brycheiniog, the land of Brychan, a fifth-century ruler.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Brecon is the county town of Brycheiniog in mid-Wales, standing where the Honddu meets the Usk under the high moorland of the Beacons. It had a Benedictine priory that became the parish church and later the cathedral of a new diocese, and a grammar school refounded in the sixteenth century. Its standing in the dictionary rests on one farm. Trevecca, in the parish of Talgarth in Breconshire, was the home of Howell Harris, who was converted at Talgarth church at Whitsun 1735 while receiving the Lord's Supper and began almost at once to exhort his neighbours house by house. Harris was never ordained; he was refused orders four times, and his work was therefore irregular from the start, carried on in houses, barns and open fields and organised into societies with appointed exhorters over them. The same year and without knowledge of him, Daniel Rowland was awakened in Cardiganshire; the two met in 1737, and the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist movement dates from their joining. Harris later gathered a community at Trevecca and the Countess of Huntingdon placed her college there in 1768. The dictionary records Brecon as the ground where a layman began what the bishops had declined to commission.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to revive as to return to life or vigour; to exhort as to incite by words; a society as a number of persons united; a beacon as a signal fire on a height; and refreshing as the act of reviving.

expand to see more

REVIVE, v.t. To return to life; to recover new life or vigour; to be reanimated after apparent death.

EXHORT, v.t. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge to any good action, especially to the practice of virtue and piety.

SOCIETY, n. A number of persons united, either for mutual benefit, or for the promotion of a particular object.

BEACON, n. A signal erected on an eminence, consisting of a pitch barrel or fire, to notice the approach of an enemy.

REFRESHING, n. The act of refreshing; relief after fatigue or suffering; new vigour or animation.

Key Scripture

Psa 85:6 — "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?"

Hab 3:2 — "O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy."

Act 3:19 — "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;"

Isa 44:3 — "For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:"

Modern Corruption

Mid-Welsh county town under the Beacons, holding Trevecca where Howell Harris was converted in 1735 and began the unordained exhorting out of which Welsh Calvinistic Methodism grew.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the modern manufacture of revival, the assumption that what happened at Talgarth and Llangeitho can be arranged by method, atmosphere and sufficient expectation. The Welsh awakening began with two men in two counties who did not know of each other, and the dictionary holds that this is the ordinary shape of the thing. Scripture asks for it as a gift and not as a technique: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6), and Habakkuk prays “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years” (Hab 3:2) with the plea for mercy in wrath attached, which is not the language of a man expecting to produce an effect.

The second word is against the opposite error, which is the one the establishment fell into here. Harris was refused ordination four times, and the refusal did not stop the work; it only guaranteed that the work would be done outside the parish structure and would eventually leave it. Where repentance and conversion are preached the refreshing follows, for “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” (Act 3:19), and the promise of the poured-out Spirit is made to the thirsty and the dry rather than to the regular: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3). A church that will not commission its converted men should not be surprised to find them gone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chayah (H2421), to live or revive; Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn or be converted; Greek anapsuxis (G403), refreshing.

expand to see more

Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to keep alive, to revive; “Wilt thou not revive us again”, Psalm 85:6.

Hebrew po'al (H6467) — a work, a deed; “revive thy work in the midst of the years”, Habakkuk 3:2.

Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; “Repent ye therefore, and be converted”, Acts 3:19.

Greek anapsuxis (G403) — a cooling, a recovery of breath, refreshing; “the times of refreshing shall come”, Acts 3:19.

Hebrew yatsaq (H3332) — to pour out, to pour forth; “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty”, Isaiah 44:3.

Usage

"“Wilt thou not revive us again” (Psa 85:6) — Talgarth and Llangeitho in the same year, unknown to each other."

"“the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” (Act 3:19) — Harris exhorting house by house."

"“floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3) — orders refused four times and the work going on."
